questions.prompt: Why must YARA rules for memory use 'wide ascii' rather than ASCII alone?
options: ..NET and PowerShell hold strings as UTF-16, so an ASCII-only rule misses them entirely
questions.explanation: This is the same UTF-16LE property behind PowerShell encoded-command decoding -- a rule matching only ASCII will not find managed-code strings in memory.

questions.prompt: Why does scanning memory with YARA find things a disk scan cannot?
options: A reflectively-loaded assembly never existed as a file for a disk scan to examine, but its strings are resident in memory
YARA cannot scan disks at all
questions.explanation: This is what makes YARA effective against fileless payloads that leave no on-disk artifact whatsoever.

questions.prompt: What does a driver appearing in windows.modscan but absent from windows.modules indicate?
options: A normal driver loading race condition
An unlinked kernel module -- the same list-versus-pool-scan logic as pslist versus psscan, applied to drivers
questions.explanation: One walks a linked list and the other scans for pool tags, so a scan-only hit means the module was deliberately unlinked -- the kernel-tampering and BYOVD signature.

questions.prompt: Why is the pagefile worth collecting even when memory acquisition never happened?
options: It contains a full copy of RAM at shutdown
Paged-out memory content survives a reboot, so a machine restarted before anyone responded may still hold fragments of what was resident
It is smaller and faster to analyze
It contains the Windows event logs
questions.explanation: Unlike RAM, the pagefile persists across reboots -- and while it has no memory-image structure, it is directly scannable with YARA and carvable with strings or bulk_extractor.
